en: Thus have I heard: the Alagaddūpama Sutta, the Discourse on the Simile of the Snake, from the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a pernicious view had arisen in a monk named Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-trainer, as follows:
“As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not actually capable of obstructing one who indulges in them.”
A number of bhikkhus heard:
"It seems that a pernicious view has arisen in the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-keeper, named thus:
'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.'"
Then those bhikkhus approached the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers; having approached, they said this to the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers:
“Is it true, friend Ariṭṭha, that such an evil speculative view has arisen in you:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them’?”

“Indeed, friends, it is in this way that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: those things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not at all able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
Then those bhikkhus, wishing to detach the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha—who had formerly been a vulture trainer—from that evil course of view, questioned him, cross-examined him, and rebuked him:
“Do not say so, friend Ariṭṭha; do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak in such a way.
In many ways, friend Ariṭṭha, the Blessed One has stated that obstructive things are indeed obstructive, and they are sufficient to create an obstacle for one who indulges in them.
The Blessed One has stated that sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger here is greater.”
“Sensual pleasures have been compared to a skeleton by the Blessed One;
sensual pleasures have been compared to a piece of meat by the Blessed One;
sensual pleasures have been compared to a torch of grass by the Blessed One.”
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like embers;
the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a dream;
the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods.
Sensual pleasures have been compared to the fruit of a tree by the Blessed One...
sensual pleasures have been compared to a sword and a butcher’s block by the Blessed One...
sensual pleasures have been compared to spears and spikes by the Blessed One...
“Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to the head of a snake; they bring much suffering and much despair, and the danger therein is even greater.

Even though the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-haunters, was thus pressed, questioned, and exhorted by those bhikkhus, he stubbornly and obstinately adhered to that same evil view and declared:
“Friends, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that these things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.”
When those bhikkhus were unable to detach the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers, from that evil course of view, they then approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, such an evil view has arisen in the bhikkhu named Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called “obstructive states” by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
We thought, venerable sir:”
“It seems, Bhante, that such an evil view has arisen in the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher, named thus:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called “obstructive states” by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
Then, Bhante, we approached the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher, and having approached him, we said this to the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher:”
“Is it true, friend Ariṭṭha, that such an evil view has arisen in you:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called “obstructive states” by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them’?
When this was said, Bhante, the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher, said this to us:

“‘Indeed, friends, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that these things called “obstructive states” by the Blessed One are not at all capable of obstructing one who indulges in them.
Then, Bhante, wishing to detach the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly afflicted by vultures, from this evil course of view, we questioned him, cross-examined him, and pressed him for an explanation.”
“Do not say so, friend Ariṭṭha; do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak in such a way.
In many ways, friend Ariṭṭha, the Blessed One has stated that the things which are obstacles are indeed obstacles, and they are sufficient to become obstacles for one who indulges in them.
The Blessed One has stated that sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger in them is greater.”
“Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a skeleton...
they have been compared by the Blessed One to the head of a snake—full of suffering, full of despair; the danger here is even greater.

Even so, Bhante, when the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers, was pressed, questioned, and cross-examined by us, he stubbornly clung to and insisted upon that same evil view, saying: [as before]... “The danger here is even greater. Thus, Bhante, while being pressed, questioned, and cross-examined by us, the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers, stubbornly clung to and insisted upon that very same evil view, asserting: [as before].

“Indeed, friend, it is in this way that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: those things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
“Venerable sir, since we were unable to detach the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers, from this evil speculative view, we have come to report this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu:
“Come, bhikkhu, in my name address the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly afflicted by vultures, saying:
‘Friend Ariṭṭha, the Teacher calls for you.

“Very well, Bhante,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One, and he approached the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly afflicted by vultures. Having approached him, he said this to the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly afflicted by vultures:
“The Teacher calls you, friend Ariṭṭha.
“Very well, friend,” the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers, replied to that bhikkhu.
He approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. To one side...
When the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly afflicted by gout, was seated, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Is it true, Ariṭṭha, that such an evil view has arisen in you:
'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not actually sufficient to obstruct one who indulges in them'?"

“Venerable sir, it is in this way that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: ‘Those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
“Whom, you foolish man, do you think has taught the Dhamma to you in such a way?
Have I not, you foolish man, in many ways declared that obstructive things are indeed obstructive? And are they not sufficient to obstruct one who indulges in them?”
"Sensual pleasures have been called 'of little gratification,' I have said, 'of much suffering and much despair; the danger therein is greater.
Sensual pleasures have been compared by me to a skeleton...
sensual pleasures have been compared by me to a piece of meat..."
"Sensual pleasures have been compared by me to a grass torch...
sensual pleasures have been compared by me to a pit of glowing coals...
sensual pleasures have been compared by me to a dream..."
Sensual pleasures have been described by me as being like borrowed goods;
sensual pleasures have been described by me as being like the fruit of a tree;
sensual pleasures have been described by me as being like a sword and a butcher’s block.
"Sensual pleasures have been described by me as being like spears and spikes...
sensual pleasures have been described by me as being like the heads of snakes—bringing much suffering, much despair; the danger therein is even greater.
Yet you, foolish man, by your own misapprehension, both misrepresent us and ruin yourself, and generate much demerit."
“For that, foolish man, will lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“What do you think, bhikkhus?”
"Could it be that this bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-keeper, has even attained the warmth [of the path] in this Dhamma and Discipline?
"How could that be, Bhante?
Certainly not, Bhante."
When this was said, the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers, sat silent, ashamed, with shoulders drooping and head bowed,
brooding and unable to respond. Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers, was silent, ashamed,
with shoulders drooping and head bowed, brooding and unable to respond, said this to him:
“You will indeed be known by this, foolish man, through your own evil adherence to wrong view.
In this matter, I shall question the bhikkhus.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Do you, monks, understand the Dhamma taught by me in such a way that this bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers,
by his own misapprehension, misrepresents us, ruins himself, and generates much demerit? “Certainly not, Bhante.”
"For in many ways, venerable sir, the Blessed One has declared that things which are obstructive are indeed obstructive;
they are sufficient to become obstacles for one who indulges in them.
The Blessed One has declared that sensual pleasures provide little gratification, but much suffering and much despair; the danger here is greater."
“Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a skeleton...
they have been compared by the Blessed One to the head of a snake—full of suffering, full of despair; the danger here is even greater.
“Excellent, excellent, monks! It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me in this way.”
"In many ways, monks, have obstructive things been described by me; they are indeed sufficient to be obstacles for one who indulges in them.
Sensual pleasures have been described by me as providing little gratification, but much suffering and much despair; the danger therein is greater.
Sensual pleasures have been described by me as being like a skeleton... [and so on].
Sensual pleasures have been compared by me to the head of a serpent; they bring much suffering and much despair, and the danger therein is even greater.
Yet this bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher, because of his own misapprehension, slanders both us and himself, and he accumulates much demerit.
For that will lead to the misfortune and suffering of that foolish man for a long time.
“Indeed, monks, that one should indulge in sensual pleasures apart from sensual desires, apart from the perception of sensual desires, and apart from thoughts of sensual desires—
that is impossible. Here, monks, certain foolish men master the Dhamma—
the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, ‘Thus-it-was-said’ passages, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and analytical teachings.”
Having mastered those teachings, they do not examine their meaning with wisdom.
Since they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom, they do not find them satisfactory upon reflection.
They master the teachings merely for the sake of finding fault and for the sake of gaining victory in debate.
They do not experience the goal for the sake of which they have mastered the Dhamma;
those teachings, being wrongly grasped by them, lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. And why is that?
“Because of misinterpreting the teachings, monks. It is just as if,
monks, a man needing a viper, seeking a viper, wandering in search of a viper,
were to see a large viper.”
One might seize it by its coils or by its tail.
That viper would turn back and bite one on the hand, the arm, or some other limb.
Because of that, one would meet death or suffering amounting to death.
And why is that? Because of their misapprehension of the *alagadda*, monks.
In the same way, monks, here some foolish men master the Dhamma—
The discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" sayings, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and questions-and-answers.
Having mastered that Dhamma, they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom.
As they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom, they do not find them satisfying through contemplation.
They master the Dhamma for the sake of finding fault and for the sake of gaining victory in debates;
yet they do not experience the purpose for which they master the Dhamma.
Since those teachings have been wrongly grasped by them, they lead to their harm and suffering for a long time.
For what reason?
Because of their misapprehension of the teachings, monks.
But here, monks, some sons of good family master the teachings:

The discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), "thus-it-was-said" (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical teachings (vedalla).
Having mastered that Dhamma, they examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom.
As they examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom, they find them acceptable through contemplation.
They do not master the Dhamma for the sake of finding fault, nor for the sake of escaping through mere sophistry;
rather, they experience the very purpose for which they master the Dhamma.
Those teachings, being well-learned by them, lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time.
And why is that? Because, monks, the teachings have been well grasped.
It is just as if, monks, a man needing a water-snake, seeking a water-snake, were wandering in search of a water-snake.
Suppose he were to see a large water-snake and,
with a forked stick, were to seize it firmly by the neck;
having seized it firmly by the neck with the forked stick, he would hold it securely by the throat.
"Even though, monks, that water-snake might wrap its coils around that man’s hand,
or arm, or any other limb, nevertheless he would not, on that account, meet death or suffering amounting to death."
And why is that? Because, monks, they have grasped the viper correctly.
In the same way, monks, here some clansmen master the Dhamma—
Discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, accounts of marvelous qualities, and analytical expositions.
Having mastered that Dhamma, they examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom.
As they examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom, they come to accept them through contemplation.
They do not master the Dhamma for the sake of finding fault, nor for the sake of gaining victory in debate;
rather, they experience that very purpose for which they master the Dhamma.
Those teachings, being well-grasped by them, lead to their welfare, benefit, and happiness for a long time.
For what reason?
Because, monks, the teachings have been well grasped.
Therefore, monks, whatever I have spoken that you understand its meaning, you should retain it accordingly.
"And if you do not understand the meaning of what I have said, you should question me about it, or those bhikkhus who are experienced.
Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma by way of a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping.
Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak."
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, it is just as if a man were traveling along a long journey.”
Suppose he were to see a vast expanse of water, with this shore being dangerous and fearful, and the far shore being safe and free from fear;
yet there were no boat for crossing, nor any bridge for going from the hither side to the further side.
It would occur to him:
‘This great expanse of water has a near shore that is dangerous and fearful, and a far shore that is safe and free from fear;
yet there is no boat for crossing, nor is there a bridge to go from the hither side to the further side.

What if I were to gather grass, sticks, branches, and foliage, bind them together into a raft, and by relying on that raft, exerting myself with hands and feet, safely cross over to the further shore?’”

Then, monks, that man, having gathered grass, sticks, branches, and foliage, would bind them together into a raft and, relying on that raft, exerting himself with hands and feet, would safely cross over to the further shore.
Once that man had crossed over and reached the further shore, it would occur to him:
"This raft has been very helpful to me."
"Relying on this raft and exerting myself with my hands and feet, I have safely crossed over to the further shore.
What if I were now to place this raft on my head or carry it on my shoulder and go wherever I wish?
What do you think, monks?
“Would that man, acting in such a way, be one who has fulfilled his duty regarding that raft?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“And how, monks, would that man be one who has fulfilled his duty regarding that raft?”
In this case, monks, when that man has crossed over and reached the further shore, it would occur to him:
"This raft was indeed very helpful to me;
by relying on this raft, and through my own exertion with hands and feet, I have safely crossed over to the further shore."
‘What if I were to haul this raft onto dry land or sink it in the water, and then depart wherever I wish?
It is by doing thus, monks, that a person would have performed their duty with respect to that raft.
In the same way, monks, I have taught the Dhamma as similar to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping.
“Bhikkhus, when you understand the Dhamma taught by me as being like a raft, even phenomena must be abandoned, let alone unwholesome things.
Bhikkhus, there are these six bases for views.
What are the six?”

In this case, monks, an uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form thus:
"This is mine, this I am, this is my self"; he regards feeling thus: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self."
One regards perception as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
one regards volitional formations as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
and whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, or examined by the mind, that too one regards as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self.’
Furthermore, regarding that standpoint of views:

"The world is the self; after passing away, I shall become permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, remaining exactly thus for all eternity"—even that he regards as "This is mine, this I am, this is my self."

But the learned noble disciple, monks, who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has seen the true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of the true persons, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of the true persons—regards form thus:
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’; regards feeling thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
One regards perception thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self";
one regards volitional formations thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self";
and whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, or examined by the mind, that too one regards thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
Furthermore, regarding that standpoint of views—namely, "The world is the self;
after passing away, I shall become permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, remaining exactly thus for all eternity"—he regards even that as:
"This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
“Thus, perceiving in this way, one does not tremble when there is nothing.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:
“Could it be, Bhante, that there might be trembling regarding what is non-existent externally?”
“It may be so, bhikkhus,” the Blessed One said.
“In this case, bhikkhus, it occurs to a certain person:
‘Alas, I had that! Alas, that is no longer mine!’”
‘It might be mine, yet alas, I do not obtain it.
He sorrows, he is weary, he laments, he beats his breast, he falls into confusion.
In this way, bhikkhu, there is agitation regarding what is non-existent externally.”
“But could there be, Bhante, non-agitation regarding what is non-existent externally?
“There could be, bhikkhus,” the Blessed One said.
“In this case, bhikkhus, it does not occur to a certain person thus:”
‘Alas, what I had has vanished! Alas, what I had is no more!
What might have been for me is not now obtained!’—he does not grieve, he does not languish, he does not lament, he does not beat his breast, and he does not fall into confusion.
“In this way, bhikkhu, there is no agitation when there is nothing external.
“Could there be, Bhante, agitation when there is nothing internal?
“There could be, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said.
“Here, bhikkhu, a certain person has such a view as this:
‘That which is the world, that is the self; after passing away, I shall become permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, remaining exactly the same for all eternity.
He hears from a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata [the teaching] regarding all bases of views, determinations, obsessions, adherences, and underlying tendencies.”

As he teaches the Dhamma for the uprooting [of all formations], for the stilling of all volitional formations, for the relinquishing of all acquisitions, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, for cessation,
and for Nibbāna, it occurs to him:
‘I shall be annihilated! I shall perish! I shall no longer exist!
He sorrows, languishes, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion.
In this way, bhikkhu, there is agitation regarding what is non-existent internally.”
“But could there be, venerable sir, non-agitation when there is nothing internal?
“There could be, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said.
“Here, bhikkhu, a certain person does not hold such a view as this:”
‘This world is the self; after passing away, I shall become permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, remaining exactly as it is for all eternity.
Then he hears from a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata about the uprooting of all bases for views, all obsessions, all adherences, and all underlying tendencies;
about the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, and...
While teaching the Dhamma for the sake of cessation and Nibbāna,
it does not occur to him:
‘I shall be annihilated, I shall perish, I shall come to non-existence.’
Thus one does not grieve, does not weary, does not lament, does not weep beating one’s breast, and does not fall into confusion.
In this way, bhikkhu, there is non-agitation regarding what is non-existent internally.
Monks, you should grasp that possession which is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and which would remain just so for all eternity.
“Do you see, monks, that possession which is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and which would remain exactly so for all eternity?
“No indeed, venerable sir.
“Good, monks.”
“Monks, I do not perceive any possession whatsoever that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and that might remain exactly as it is for all eternity.
Monks, would you cling to that grasping at a self-view such that, by clinging to that grasping at a self-view, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise?
“Monks, do you see any such grasping at a self-view such that, by clinging to that grasping at a self-view, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Good, monks.
I too, monks, do not see any grasping at a doctrine of self such that, for one who grasps at that doctrine of self, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise.”
“Monks, could one rely on such a reliance on views that, by relying on it, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise?
Do you see, monks, such a reliance on views, by relying on which sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Excellent, monks!
Indeed, monks, I do not see any reliance on views such that, by relying upon it, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise.
Or, monks, when there is a self, would there be the thought: ‘This is mine’?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Bhikkhus, when there is something belonging to a self, would the thought ‘this is my self’ occur?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Bhikkhus, when neither a self nor what belongs to a self is found to exist in truth and reality,
is this view— the position that ‘The world and the self are one and the same; after death I shall be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, remaining exactly as I am for all eternity’—
not entirely and completely a foolish doctrine?”
“What could it be for us, Bhante? For this, Bhante, would be entirely and completely the dhamma of a fool.
“What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“What do you think, bhikkhus,
regarding feeling … perception …?”
“Are volitional formations … consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:”
“Is it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“Therefore, monks, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external—”
Whether gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Whatever feeling there is … [and so on] …
Whatever kind of perception...
whatever kind of volitional formations...
whatever kind of consciousness there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle—
Whether subtle or gross, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.

Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.
Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated. One understands:
"Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.

Monks, such a monk is called one who has "thrown out the crossbar," one who has "filled in the moat," one who has "pulled up the pillar," one who is "without bolts," and one who is "noble, with banner lowered, with burden dropped, and unyoked."
And how, monks, is a monk one who has removed the crossbar?
Here, monks, a monk’s ignorance has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has removed the crossbar.
And how, monks, is a monk one whose trench has been filled in?

Here, monks, a monk’s cycle of births leading to renewed existence has been abandoned; it has been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one whose trench has been filled in.
And how, monks, is a monk one who has pulled out the pillar?
Here, monks, a monk’s craving has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has pulled out the pillar.
And how, monks, is a monk one who has no bolt?
Here, monks, a monk’s five lower fetters have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has no bolt.
And how, monks, is a monk a noble one who has lowered his banner, laid down his burden, and is detached?
Here, monks, a monk’s conceit of “I am” has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is a noble one who has lowered his banner, laid down his burden, and is detached.
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus liberated, the devas together with Indra, Brahmā, and Pajāpati, though searching for it, do not find it, thinking:
‘Upon what is the Tathāgata’s consciousness dependent? And why is that?”
“Bhikkhus, I say that one cannot find the Tathāgata even in this very life.
When I speak thus and declare this, bhikkhus, some recluses and brahmins falsely, vainly, and untruthfully misrepresent me with what is non-existent, saying:
‘The recluse Gotama is an annihilationist; he teaches the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.’”
And it is not, monks, because I say what I do not say, that those venerable recluses and brahmins falsely, vainly, and untruthfully misrepresent me with what is non-existent, saying:
"The recluse Gotama is a nihilist; he proclaims the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
Both formerly, monks, and now, I proclaim only suffering and the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, monks, if others abuse, revile, irritate, or harass the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata feels no resentment, no ill will, and no dissatisfaction of mind.
And in that regard, monks, if others honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata feels no elation, no joy, and no mental exultation.
In that case, monks, if others honor, revere, respect, and worship the Tathāgata, it occurs to the Tathāgata:
"These such services are being performed for me regarding that which was previously fully understood.
Therefore, monks, even if others should revile you, abuse you, irritate you, or harass you, you should not harbor resentment, ill will, or mental dissatisfaction toward them.
Therefore, monks, even if others should honor you, revere you, esteem you, and worship you, you should not feel delight, joy, or mental exultation on that account.
Therefore, monks, even if others should honor you, revere you, esteem you, and worship you, you should think:
"These kinds of services are being performed for me because this was previously fully understood by me."
Therefore, monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it.
When that is abandoned, it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
And what, monks, is not yours?
“Bhikkhus, form is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned by you, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Feeling, bhikkhus, is not yours; abandon it.”
When that has been abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Perception, monks, is not yours; abandon it.
When it has been abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
“Formations, monks, are not yours; abandon them.
When they are abandoned by you, they will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Consciousness, monks, is not yours; abandon it.”
That being abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
What do you think, monks?
If people were to carry away the grass, wood, branches, and foliage in this Jeta Grove, or burn it, or do with it as they please—what would that amount to for you?"
“Would it ever occur to you:
‘People are carrying us away, or burning us, or doing with us as they please’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“And for what reason?
“Because that, Bhante, is neither our self nor what belongs to our self.
“In the same way, monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it;”
That which has been abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
And what, monks, is not yours?
Form, monks, is not yours; abandon it.
That being abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Feeling, monks... Perception, monks...
"Formations, monks... consciousness, monks, is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned by you, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time."

"Thus, monks, has the Dhamma been well-expounded by me— clear, open, revealed, with its shrouds cut away. Since the Dhamma has been thus well-expounded by me, clear, open, revealed, and with its shrouds cut away,
those monks who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, and attained their own goal— "
With the fetters of existence utterly destroyed, they are liberated through right knowledge; for them, there is no further round to be described.
Thus, monks, has the Dhamma been well-expounded by me—clear, open, revealed, with its bark-fiber stripped away.
Monks, since the Dhamma has been thus well-expounded by me, clear, open, revealed, and with its bark-fiber stripped away, for those...
"Bhikkhus, for those bhikkhus who have abandoned the five lower fetters, all of them are of spontaneous birth; they will attain final nibbāna there and are not subject to return from that world.
Thus, bhikkhus, has the Dhamma been well-expounded by me—made plain, revealed, and clarified, with its bark-fiber removed."
"Monks, when the Dhamma has been thus well-expounded by me— clear, revealed, made manifest, with its shrouds cut away—
those monks who have abandoned the three fetters and attenuated lust, hatred, and delusion are all once-returners;
having returned to this world only once more, they will make an end of suffering."
“Monks, thus has the Dhamma been well-expounded by me— clear, open, revealed, with its shrouds cut away. Monks,
since the Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, clear, open, revealed, and with its shrouds cut away,
those monks who have abandoned the three fetters are all stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as their final goal.”
“Thus, monks, has the Dhamma been well-expounded by me—clear, open, revealed, with its shrouds cut away.

Since the Dhamma has been thus well-expounded by me, clear, open, revealed, with its shrouds cut away, those monks who are followers of the Dhamma and followers by faith—all of them have enlightenment as their ultimate goal.
Thus, monks, has the Dhamma been well-expounded by me—clear, open, revealed, with its shrouds cut away.”

“Monks, when the Dhamma has been thus well-expounded by me—proclaimed, revealed, made manifest, with its bark stripped away—all those who possess even a measure of faith and a measure of affection for me are destined for heaven.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Elated, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Discourse on the Simile of the Snake is finished; the second [in this section].
